edges.description: Both decompose the problem hierarchically; coarsening levels ↔ frontier partition depth
Frontier partitions define natural batches; lazy propagation handles inter-partition corrections
Spectral embedding provides the potential function; both reduce effective problem size
Wavefront propagation is inherently local; LSR formalizes and exploits this locality
Entropy bounds determine phase of computational difficulty; phase transitions mark entropy discontinuities
Filtration levels ↔ coarsening levels; both build nested approximations
Potentials define batch boundaries (equi-potential surfaces); lazy propagation handles corrections within batches
Spectral coarsening (top eigenvectors) naturally defines the multigrid hierarchy for graphs

bridge_chains.insight: Spectral coarsening provides both the multigrid hierarchy and the potential functions. The coarsest level gives a global potential; each refinement level adds local corrections. This three-concept bridge suggests: compute spectral potentials at coarse levels, use them to guide fine-level SSSP, achieving sub-logarithmic correction cost per level.

Frontier partitioning creates batches; entropy analysis of each batch determines its computational budget. Batches with low distance-entropy (well-ordered distances) are processed cheaply; high-entropy batches get more comparisons. This adaptive budgeting could improve the log^{2/3}(n) factor in Duan et al. by spending fewer comparisons on easy partitions.

Build a weight-based filtration, propagate wavefronts within each filtration level using locality-sensitive ordering. New edges added at each filtration level cause only local wavefront perturbations. This suggests: SSSP via incremental wavefront maintenance across a filtration, with O(m) total perturbation cost + O(n · f(log n)) for wavefront reordering.
